name: Myositis ossificans traumatica
aliases: pseudomalignant osseous tumour of soft tissue

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A benign, self-limiting formation of heterotopic bone within skeletal muscle, usually following trauma in young active adults
Presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, tender soft-tissue mass, often in the thigh, buttock or upper arm
The defining feature is zonal maturation, with a mineralising peripheral shell of mature bone surrounding a cellular, immature central zone
This zonal pattern is the reverse of osteosarcoma, in which the most immature and dense mineralisation tends to lie centrally
Radiographic ossification typically becomes visible several weeks after injury and matures peripherally over time
Early biopsy can be dangerously misleading, as the immature cellular centre mimics a sarcoma histologically
Management is usually conservative with observation, as the lesion matures and often partially regresses without excision
reference.pathophysiology: Myositis ossificans traumatica is a benign, reactive proliferation of fibroblasts, cartilage and bone within soft tissue, most often triggered by a single injury or repetitive microtrauma. Local tissue damage initiates a proliferative fibroblastic response that undergoes progressive metaplastic differentiation into cartilage and then bone. The lesion matures in a centripetal, zonal fashion, with the peripheral rim ossifying first and most completely, while the centre remains cellular and immature early in the course. Over weeks to months the whole lesion becomes better demarcated and ossified, and it may shrink.
additionalInvestigations: Serial plain radiography to demonstrate evolving peripheral ossification over time
CT to display the characteristic peripheral mineralised rim and central lucency
MRI to assess the soft-tissue mass, noting surrounding oedema in early lesions
Correlation of imaging with time since injury to recognise the maturation sequence
Biopsy only when imaging is atypical, ideally deferred until the lesion has matured
redFlags: A mass without peripheral maturation raising concern for extraskeletal osteosarcoma
Continued growth beyond the expected maturation window
Central rather than peripheral dense mineralisation on imaging
Absence of any traumatic history with atypical imaging features
reference.prognosis: Myositis ossificans is benign and self-limiting, typically maturing and stabilising over several months, often with partial resorption. Excision, if required for symptoms, is best delayed until the lesion is mature to reduce recurrence, and the outlook is excellent.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the cellular immature centre on early biopsy as a sarcoma
Reversing the zonal reasoning and mistaking it for extraskeletal osteosarcoma
Excising a lesion prematurely before maturation, increasing recurrence risk
Imaging too early before diagnostic peripheral ossification has developed
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
